verdicts.text: Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3 (temporal claim; SST v3 may already have been released, given the post was updated 2025-03-05).
verdicts.evidence: The line correctly quotes SST's Jan 2024 post ("Once Ion is stable, it'll be released as SST v3"), but it is out of date. SST's own v3 announcement (Aug 20, 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3", so describing the release as a future event is wrong for a post updated 2025-03-05.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source made a plan in Jan 2024 ("it'll be released as SST v3"). The 2025 post repeats it as a pending future event, but it already happened (Ion became SST v3 on Aug 20, 2024).

verdicts.text: The SST team expanded focus beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, which is why AWS-centric CDK became a limitation.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post backs the multi-cloud reason: "there is now genuine demand from the SST community wanting to use Cloudflare," and with CDK & CFN "we'd have to create Custom Resources for these providers." Nothing in SST's post or its v3 announcement mentions on-premises infrastructure. The v3 README's wording is "Native support for non-AWS providers."
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the claim widens the source's 'other providers... Most notably Cloudflare' to 'other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure'
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'On-premises' doesn't fit a serverless-focused framework like SST; it looks like the author added it.

verdicts.text: SST (Serverless Stack) is a framework for building modern full-stack applications, and was originally built on top of AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own v3 announcement says "SST was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation," and its Ion post talks about "a new version of SST that's not based on CDK." SST's docs also describe building full-stack apps.
verdicts.framing_note: Source says 'SST was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation'; claim says 'originally built on top of AWS CDK'.

verdicts.text: Multi-cloud deployments were nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
verdicts.evidence: Independent sources confirm that AWS CDK only works with AWS: Encore says "CDK is AWS only", and SST's v3 migration docs contrast CDK with Pulumi's "150+ other providers that allow you to build on any cloud." "Nearly impossible" is the author's descriptive wording, but it fits the fact that CDK synthesizes to AWS CloudFormation.
verdicts.framing_note: Descriptive characterization; the underlying fact (CDK is AWS-only via CloudFormation) is well established. The live pulumi.com copy of this post was not used as evidence.

verdicts.text: The in-article table-of-contents links point to anchors on the post's aliased URL /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/ (#the-beginnings-of-sst, #cdk-and-cloudformation-limitations, etc.), which must resolve to the matching headings.
verdicts.evidence: The front matter has `aliases: - /blog/from-cdk-pulumi-evolution-of-sst/`. All six TOC anchors match H2 headings in the same file: "## The Beginnings of SST" (L83), "## CDK and CloudFormation Limitations" (L89), "## A Provider-agnostic Solution: Discovering Pulumi" (L110), "## Transitioning to Pulumi" (L120), "## The Benefits of Pulumi" (L128) and "## The Future of SST with Pulumi" (L162).
verdicts.intuition_flag: The links point to the alias URL, not the canonical /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/. If the alias is a Hugo meta-refresh page, the #fragment may be lost on redirect. Changing the links to same-page anchors (#...) would be safer.

verdicts.text: The SST team concluded that limitations of CDK and AWS CloudFormation were holding them back from empowering application developers.
verdicts.evidence: SST's "Moving away from CDK" post explains that CloudFormation is an opaque black box: "As a framework author that's trying to build a better developer experience on AWS, this limits what we can do. And this turns out to be a deal-breaker." The post also covers "underlying design flaws with the CDK & CFN model."
verdicts.framing_note: Paraphrase: the source says CDK/CFN limits "build a better developer experience on AWS"; the claim says the limitations were "holding them back from empowering application developers." The meaning is the same, only the wording differs.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
verdicts.evidence: The claim holds, but it doesn't list every language AWS CDK supports. Pulumi's own CDK comparison page lists CDK language support as "TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, C#, and Java", so TypeScript and Python are both included. This is well-known public fact, but a same-site page is corroboration only, not independent authority.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names two of the six supported languages. It reads as a partial list rather than an exclusive one, so it's still accurate.

verdicts.text: AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator, producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code a developer writes is not the code running during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: AWS CDK docs: "Stack synthesis is the process of producing an AWS CloudFormation template and deployment artifacts from a CDK stack... The cloud assembly is what gets deployed to provision your resources on AWS." The template is output in YAML, and CloudFormation deploys that template, not the developer's code.
verdicts.framing_note: Strictly speaking, CDK is the code generator and CloudFormation is the engine that runs the generated JSON/YAML template. Grouping "CDK and CloudFormation" together is a loose shorthand, but the core claim (an intermediate template is what gets deployed) is supported.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi docs page at /docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/#what-is-aws-cloudformation exists and describes AWS CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: The target page exists, and its heading "## What is AWS CloudFormation?" (L37) produces the anchor #what-is-aws-cloudformation. The section describes the service: "AWS CloudFormation is an AWS-managed service for provisioning AWS resources from templates written in JSON or YAML."

verdicts.text: The SST team expanded its focus beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, and found the AWS-centric nature of CDK and CloudFormation a limitation.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post supports the move beyond AWS: it says Cloudflare now has "genuine demand from the SST community", and that "with the current CDK & CFN model we'd have to create Custom Resources for these providers." None of the SST text I retrieved mentions on-premises infrastructure. The on-prem part appears only in the pre-change copy of the Pulumi post under review.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: SST's source talks about non-AWS providers like Cloudflare, but the claim adds 'on-premises infrastructure', which SST doesn't mention in the retrieved text
verdicts.intuition_flag: SST is a serverless/cloud framework, so on-premises infrastructure seems out of character for it and looks like an embellishment by the author.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi docs page https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/ has a section 'what-is-aws-cdk' describing the AWS-centric nature of CDK.
verdicts.evidence: The target page has a heading "## What is AWS CDK?" (anchor #what-is-aws-cdk), and that section says "CDK is AWS-only" and describes it as "an AWS-maintained framework ... for defining AWS infrastructure".

verdicts.text: Pulumi does not generate an intermediary format; it treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's architecture guide says that during `pulumi up`, "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program." As each resource is constructed, "the language host sends a _resource registration_ request to the deployment engine and then continues executing the program." So the program runs directly while the deployment happens, and no intermediate template is generated (unlike CDK's CloudFormation synthesis).
verdicts.framing_note: The docs describe live execution through the language host and gRPC resource registration. "No intermediary format" is an accurate summary: Pulumi uses no template like CloudFormation, although the engine does record state.

verdicts.text: With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that is running during deployment, giving greater visibility into the deployment process and ability to extend or customize it.
verdicts.evidence: The docs back up the factual part of the claim, that the Pulumi program itself runs during deployment: "the Pulumi CLI launches the ... language host and requests that it execute the program ... The language host continues to execute your program concurrently with the engine processing this request." The claims of "greater visibility" and extensibility are the blog's own comparison with CDK's generate-a-template approach, which is opinion and can't be checked.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim describes SST's reasons for switching. The architecture fact is confirmed; the benefits are qualitative opinion.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach lets SST's team easily work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.
verdicts.evidence: The capability part checks out: Pulumi ships providers for cloud and on-premises platforms. For example, pulumi/pulumi-vsphere is described as "A Pulumi resource package for VMWare VSphere, providing multi-language access to vCenter Server and ESXi", and it sits alongside the AWS, Azure and GCP providers. How "easily" SST's team works with them is a subjective testimonial about SST's experience and can't be checked.
verdicts.framing_note: This is a general capability claim with no cited source. The "easily" wording is marketing language.

verdicts.text: SST had built higher-level components and abstractions on top of CDK and had to re-implement them for Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post says Ion components "are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi" while looking "roughly the same" as before, and that CDK constructs can't be used in Ion. SST's v2 migration guide adds that the Pulumi/Terraform ecosystem "is mainly made up of low level resources." Together these back the claim that SST rebuilt its higher-level components on Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's sources don't use the word "re-implement." They say the same components are now defined on Terraform providers/Pulumi and CDK constructs can't be carried over, which implies the rebuild.

verdicts.text: The SST team aimed for the Pulumi-based version of SST to match the functionality of the CDK-based version and improve on it.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's announcement says of Ion, the Pulumi-based engine: "The components look roughly the same as they do today and it'll still be completely open source," and the post lays out the CDK/CloudFormation flaws Ion was built to fix. SST never states a "match the functionality and improve on it" goal in those words, so this is a reasonable paraphrase rather than a direct quote. The v3 post also admits some v2 constructs (Job, Auth, EventBus) weren't supported at launch.
verdicts.framing_note: SST's own post says components "look roughly the same" as before, plus it lists improvements (speed, no rollbacks, no CDK conflicts). The claim reads that as an aim to "match functionality and improve on it", which is an inferred paraphrase rather than a stated goal.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Match the functionality" is stronger than SST's "roughly the same", and at v3 launch some v2 constructs still weren't supported, so avoid implying full feature parity.

verdicts.text: The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
verdicts.evidence: An exact-phrase search turned up no independent source for this quote. The only place it appears is the published copy of the page under review, and that can't verify itself. Pulumi's PulumiUP 2024 agenda lists "Dax Raad (Founding Engineer, SST)" giving the talk "From CDK to Pulumi: Evolution of SST", so the quote probably comes from that talk, but no transcript turned up to check the wording.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "\"deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code\""; top results didn't address the claim. Context: https://www.pulumi.com/blog/pulumiup-global-cloud-iac-platform-engineering-ai-conference/
verdicts.intuition_flag: The quote reads like polished marketing copy and is credited to a job title rather than a name (Dax Raad). The reviewer should check it against the PulumiUP talk recording or a written approval from SST.

verdicts.text: Because Pulumi infrastructure code is the deployment code, SST developers could easily trace issues back to the source and understand what was happening during deployment.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own "Moving away from CDK" post says of the Pulumi-based engine, "The code you write is what's being executed and deployed," and adds "we are not dealing with the CloudFormation black box." That backs the basic point that the infrastructure code is the deployment code, so debugging is more transparent. The words "easily trace issues back to the source" are the blog's own paraphrase, not SST's wording.
verdicts.framing_note: Paraphrase: SST says "code you write is what's being executed" and "not dealing with the CloudFormation black box"; the claim puts this as "easily trace issues back to the source." That is a slightly stronger phrasing, but the meaning is the same.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Insights (https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments.
verdicts.evidence: /product/pulumi-insights/ is now an alias that redirects to the Discovery & governance page (content/product/discovery-governance.md). That page does promise visibility, but it means cloud resource search and compliance: "Pulumi discovers all resources, including those created outside infrastructure-as-code, providing complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting." It says nothing about debugging deployments. The blog credits that ability to the program code being the same as the deployment code, which is how the IaC engine works, not an Insights feature.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — the page offers 'complete visibility for governance and troubleshooting' of cloud resources; the claim says 'improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployments'. The link also redirects to a renamed product page (Discovery & governance).
verdicts.intuition_flag: Both links (L136, L169) use Insights as the citation for deployment debugging and observability; a link to the IaC or deployment docs may fit better.

verdicts.text: The SST team used Pulumi's extensibility features to integrate with a wide range of cloud and on-premises services and implement complex deployment workflows.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post confirms it built Ion "with the Pulumi deployment engine and their bridged Terraform providers," and third-party write-ups say this gave SST access to all Pulumi packages and multi-cloud linking (AWS, Cloudflare, Vercel). No source I found says SST integrated with "on-premises services" or used Pulumi to "implement complex deployment workflows."
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the sources support 'bridged Terraform providers / all Pulumi packages / multi-cloud', but the claim widens this to 'a wide range of cloud and on-premises services' plus 'complex deployment workflows'
verdicts.intuition_flag: Generic marketing phrasing ('cloud and on-premises', 'complex deployment workflows') is odd for SST, a serverless/cloud framework, and reads as LLM filler rather than something SST said.

verdicts.text: Pulumi has built-in extensibility features, including custom providers and dynamic components (dynamic providers/component resources).
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi docs say "Pulumi also supports dynamic providers in TypeScript and Python, which let you declare custom resources inline within a Pulumi program." The Resources page describes a ComponentResource as "a logical grouping of other resources that creates a larger, higher-level abstraction". Custom providers (bridged/native) are documented as well. "Dynamic components" isn't a Pulumi term, but the parenthetical clarifies it means dynamic providers plus component resources, and both exist.
verdicts.framing_note: Loose wording: "dynamic components" isn't a Pulumi term, but the parenthetical maps it to real features (dynamic providers, component resources).

verdicts.text: With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired customization.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own post ("Moving away from CDK") says CloudFormation is a black box: "You cannot customize it as a user and as we'll see later, neither can CDK." It also describes workarounds, such as setting up custom domains or storing URLs for a Lambda to fetch later. However, it does not describe SST as often resorting to "hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions". That wording appears only on the published copy of the reviewed Pulumi post, which can't verify itself.
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/blog/moving-away-from-cdk/ ; WebSearch ran query "sst.dev \"Moving away from CDK\" custom resources Lambda CloudFormation limitations"
verdicts.framing_note: SST's source says CFN/CDK can't be customized and gives specific workarounds; the claim adds "often" and "custom Lambda functions" as SST's regular practice, which SST's post doesn't say.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This sentence reads like Pulumi paraphrasing SST, not something SST said. The same post also has first-person slips ("our users' requirements"), which suggests the text was ghost-written or reworded.

verdicts.text: With Pulumi, the SST team was able to add support for new providers, and SST users can deploy across multiple clouds and on-premises through a single consistent interface.
verdicts.evidence: SST's v3 migration docs point users to Pulumi's AWS provider and note that "There are also 150+ other providers that allow you to build on any cloud." SST's own post says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi." Together these support the claims about new provider support and multi-cloud deployment. The "on-premises" part isn't stated directly.
verdicts.framing_note: SST says '150+ other providers that allow you to build on any cloud'; the claim restates this as multi-cloud support through new providers and adds 'on-premises', which SST doesn't mention.
verdicts.intuition_flag: SST's sources don't mention 'on-premises' deployment or 'a single consistent interface'. These may be the blog author's own additions.

verdicts.text: With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure (across multiple cloud providers and on-premises) through a single, consistent interface without juggling multiple tools.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own provider docs confirm the multi-cloud, single-config part of the claim: "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers. This includes the major clouds like AWS, Azure, and GCP". Nothing I found from SST mentions on-premises infrastructure. That part is only inferred, from Pulumi/Terraform having providers such as vSphere and Kubernetes.
verdicts.framing_note: SST docs describe support for multiple providers and clouds. The claim goes further with "all of their infrastructure (across multiple cloud providers and on-premises)", and on-prem is not stated by SST.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "All of their infrastructure… and on-premises" is marketing language that goes beyond what SST documents. Consider softening it or dropping "on-premises".

verdicts.text: SST users can write their infrastructure logic in the same programming languages they use for their application code.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own docs say "your entire app is defined in code — in a single sst.config.ts file," so infrastructure is written only in TypeScript. Application functions, however, can use JS/TS, Python, Go, C#, Rust and containers. That means the claim only holds for teams whose app code is also TypeScript/JavaScript. It does not hold across "the same programming languages" in general.
verdicts.framing_note: SST infra = TypeScript only (sst.config.ts); the multi-language support covers function runtimes, not infrastructure definitions.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The plural "languages" suggests SST supports multiple infrastructure languages, but it is TS-only. Suggested rewording: "in TypeScript, the same language as much of their application code".

verdicts.text: Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
verdicts.evidence: Pulumi's IaC docs say the "open source infrastructure as code SDK supports TypeScript, Python, Go, .NET, Java, YAML, and HCL" and let you "Manage infrastructure across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and thousands of cloud providers." Third-party write-ups (DZone, Medium) say the same about languages and multi-cloud/hybrid support. None of the fetched sources explicitly say "on-premises," though Kubernetes and other providers cover that case.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names only four of the supported languages (the source also lists Java, YAML, and HCL), and that shorter list is still true. "On-premises" isn't stated word-for-word in the sources; it follows from the Kubernetes and hybrid provider support.

verdicts.text: The SST team is exploring deeper integration with application frameworks and expanded provider support for cloud and on-premises providers built on Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: The only source that states this roadmap is the live published copy of the page under review, which lists "Deeper Integration with Application Frameworks" and "Expanded Provider Support". That can't count as independent evidence. No SST-owned source (sst.dev docs or blog) in the results describes these future plans. sst.dev does confirm SST is built on Pulumi and supports 150+ providers.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "SST roadmap Pulumi providers framework integration"; only https://www.pulumi.com/blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ (the reviewed page) addressed it
verdicts.intuition_flag: This attributes forward-looking intent to the SST team, based on a 2024 post. The roadmap may be stale by 2026, and no primary SST statement was found.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud Deployments (linked docs page /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/) provides advanced deployment workflows, and SST can use them to deliver faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and more granular control over deployment.
verdicts.evidence: Line 168 is a future-looking statement about SST's plans: "Building on Pulumi's extensibility, they can create [more advanced deployment workflows](.../deployments/) that address ... faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and more granular control". That describes what the SST team might build, not a claim that Pulumi Deployments already offers those capabilities, so there is nothing here to verify. I couldn't confirm the linked docs path in this repo because content/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/_index.md doesn't exist. It may redirect through an alias, so a reviewer should check the link.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the post says SST "can create more advanced deployment workflows" (future plan); the extracted claim says Pulumi Deployments "provides" them
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link target /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ isn't in the repo at that path. Check that it redirects and isn't a 404.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
verdicts.evidence: The link target exists and still carries the old Crosswalk URLs as aliases (`/docs/reference/crosswalk/aws/`, `/docs/guides/crosswalk/aws/`), so it really is the successor to the old Crosswalk guide. But the page no longer mentions Crosswalk or "day one" anywhere in its text. It now just reads "This section contains guides for working with AWS services using Pulumi" and points readers to "Choosing a Pulumi AWS provider".
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — the page says it is a general index of AWS guides; the blog says it describes how Crosswalk simplifies "day one" tasks
verdicts.intuition_flag: The "Crosswalk for AWS" name looks dropped from the docs (it only survives in URL aliases), so this conclusion bullet is probably stale wording that should be updated.

verdicts.text: An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled "Getting Stated with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
verdicts.evidence: The workshop does exist. It is defined in content/events/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/index.md with `title: Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS`, `event_type: workshop`, `url_slug: getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws`, an ungated youtube_url and a 2023 date, so it is on demand. The link text in the blog has a typo, though: it says "Getting Stated", not "Getting Started". Fix the typo to match the workshop's real title.
verdicts.source: repo:content/events/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/index.md (L3, L27-33); gh search code --repo pulumi/docs getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws
verdicts.framing_note: Source title 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' vs link text 'Getting Stated with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' (typo)
verdicts.intuition_flag: I didn't confirm that the /resources/<slug> URL resolves. The content file sits under /events/, and I'm assuming event pages render under /resources/ based on the url_slug field.

verdicts.text: Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering and DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Web search could not confirm that https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming exists or lists upcoming Platform Engineering & DevOps workshops. The "Platform Engineering & DevOps Series" appears only in older promo copy: "In-person events & virtual workshops from July 16 to Oct 31 in cities worldwide." Pulumi now lists current workshops at https://www.pulumi.com/events/.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Pulumi upcoming workshops platform engineering resources"; https://www.pulumi.com/blog/platform-engineering-devops-event-meetup-community/; https://www.pulumi.com/events/
verdicts.intuition_flag: This looks like an old promo banner for the 2024 Platform Engineering & DevOps Series (July 16 to Oct 31). The /resources/#upcoming anchor may be stale or redirect to /events/.

verdicts.text: The Pulumi signup page is at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
verdicts.evidence: Line 180 links "[try Pulumi](https://app.pulumi.com/signup)". Other pages link to the same URL, including content/confirmation/workshop.md, content/blog/pulumi-hearts-opensource, and content/events/building-containers-azure, and scripts/redirects/signup-redirects.txt redirects "signup/index.html|https://app.pulumi.com/signup".

verdicts.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists on the Pulumi blog at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/.
verdicts.evidence: content/blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/index.md exists, with title: "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" and draft: false. That file path serves at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The target post is dated 2026-09-16. If that date is still in the future when this publishes, the link could 404 until the post goes live.

verdicts.text: SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure easy.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own GitHub repo description says: "Build full-stack apps on your own infrastructure." The FAQ line restates SST's self-description. The word "easy" is marketing and can't be checked. Note that line 189 says "on your infrastructure," while the claim text says "on your own infrastructure."
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "Build full-stack apps on your own infrastructure." Claim: "framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy." Same core statement; the claim adds the subjective word "easy."

verdicts.text: Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own blog says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications." It adds that components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)." The SST v3 post confirms that Ion was later released as v3.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation". The claim leaves out the Terraform-providers part, but what it does say (deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK/CFN) is fully backed by the source.

verdicts.text: SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: SST's official docs say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim closely paraphrases SST's own FAQ answer on sst.dev/docs.

verdicts.text: SST relies primarily on SaaS revenue through its managed platform and potentially supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.
verdicts.evidence: SST does sell a paid managed Console. Its docs say "the Console will be priced based on the number of active resources in your SST apps", and the free tier covers workspaces with 350 active resources or fewer. No public source breaks down SST's revenue, so "relies primarily on SaaS revenue" can't be checked. The "enterprise services and consulting" part is hedged guesswork that no source supports.
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/docs/console/ ; https://sst.dev/blog/console-pricing-update/ ; WebSearch ran query "SST serverless stack business model revenue Console pricing"
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim guesses at a private company's revenue mix ("primarily", "potentially ... consulting"). Consider narrowing it to the checkable fact that SST sells a paid Console alongside its open-source framework.

verdicts.text: The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
verdicts.evidence: The official SST Console docs say "The Console is completely optional and comes with a free tier." The current free tier covers workspaces with 350 active resources or fewer.
verdicts.framing_note: SST docs: "completely optional and comes with a free tier". Claim: "optional and includes a free tier".

verdicts.text: SST potentially has supplemental income streams such as enterprise services and consulting.
verdicts.evidence: None of the public sources I found say SST sells enterprise services or consulting. Profiles describe it only as an open-source framework, with about $1.12M in seed funding from YC, Greylock and SV Angel (Tracxn). Northflank says the team has moved to OpenCode under Anomaly Co. Because the claim only says SST "potentially" has these income streams, it is guesswork that can't be checked either way.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "SST serverless stack business model revenue enterprise consulting"; top results (tracxn.com, crunchbase.com, northflank.com) didn't address enterprise services/consulting
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim is hedged guesswork about a third party's revenue and has no source. The paid product SST is actually known for is the SST Console, not consulting. Consider cutting the line or backing it with a source.

verdicts.evidence: This line is the blog post's own front-matter publish date (`date: 2026-09-16`). It is page metadata the author sets, not a factual claim that an outside source could confirm or contradict.

verdicts.text: SST v3 replaced AWS CDK (and CloudFormation) with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own blog says Ion (released as SST v3) components "are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)". It also says SST built its deploy experience with "the Pulumi deployment engine and their bridged Terraform providers", with nothing else to install, and that Terraform providers "are basically calls to the AWS SDK."
verdicts.framing_note: Every part of the claim appears in SST's first-party posts. The only gloss is "embedded": the source says the Pulumi engine is included in the single globally installed SST CLI, with nothing else to install.

verdicts.text: Cross-reference: the blog post /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists, is titled "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi", and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
verdicts.evidence: The file exists and is published (draft: false), with `title: "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi"`. Its body says "we'll explore why SST moved to Pulumi, what challenges they overcame", written around the SST team's experience with CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.framing_note: A Pulumi author (sara-huddleston) wrote the post, but it tells the story from the SST team's point of view, so "from SST's side" is a fair description.

verdicts.text: Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
verdicts.evidence: Defang's pulumi-defang README says its CD program "receives a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up` (or `destroy` etc.) to (de)provision the resources in it." Nitric's AWS cloud provider (nitrictech/nitric cloud/aws/go.mod) depends on github.com/pulumi/pulumi/sdk/v3 and the pulumi-aws, awsx, and docker SDKs, so its direct deployments go through Pulumi. The same go.mod also lists cdktf, which means Nitric offers Terraform-based providers too.
verdicts.framing_note: For Defang, the README states the claim directly. For Nitric, the evidence is Pulumi SDK dependencies in its provider code, not a direct quote. Nitric also ships Terraform (cdktf) providers, so saying it deploys through Pulumi is true of its Pulumi-based providers, not every Nitric deployment path.

verdicts.text: SST's release cadence and its dependency on the Pulumi engine have not changed as a result of the team's attention broadening to opencode; SST is not being abandoned.
verdicts.evidence: Outside sources back up "not abandoned," but they contradict the claim that release cadence is unchanged. Northflank says "SST development slowed in 2025 after the team shifted focus to OpenCode," and bex.co (Aug 2026) says SST "has been in maintenance mode since 2025: critical fixes still ship." Pulumi's own follow-up PR #21673 also says it "Verified... that SST is in maintenance mode with the team's active attention on opencode (not abandoned)."
verdicts.framing_note: Only the 'not abandoned' part holds up. The 'cadence unchanged' part conflicts with third-party reports that development slowed and SST is in maintenance mode. Both outside sources are competitor blogs, which is why confidence is medium.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A sibling Pulumi PR (#21673) calls SST 'in maintenance mode,' so this post's 'nothing changed' framing doesn't match other Pulumi content either.

verdicts.text: The `sst` npm package is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026, per the npm downloads API).
verdicts.evidence: Wrong target: the claim cites the npm downloads API, but the pre-fetched page is opencode.ai. That page returned HTTP 200 and says nothing about weekly downloads of the `sst` npm package. Its only usage figure is "With over 208,000 GitHub stars, 950 contributors, and over 13,000 commits, OpenCode is used and trusted by over 16M developers every month."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is tied to the npm downloads API (api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/2026-09-05:2026-09-11/sst), not to opencode.ai. The fetched page is a neighboring link and was not used for a framing check.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A reviewer should query the npm downloads API directly to confirm 796,291 for the week of 2026-09-05 to 2026-09-11.

verdicts.text: SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers: SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket and SST does not require a Pulumi account.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own state docs say: "The state is generated locally but is backed up to your provider using: A **bucket** to store the state, typically named `sst-state-<hash>`," with the passphrase stored in SSM. No Pulumi Cloud backend or Pulumi account is mentioned. One caveat: `home` can also be `cloudflare`, so an S3 bucket is only the AWS case.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs say state is backed up to the user's `home` provider (aws or cloudflare). The claim says 'S3 bucket', which only holds when `home` is aws. The 'no Pulumi account' part is inferred because the docs never mention one, not stated outright.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers' is absolute. Some SST users may also be Pulumi Cloud customers; what the sources support is that SST doesn't require Pulumi Cloud.

verdicts.text: The SST team has said, repeatedly since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine (embedded engine plus Terraform-bridged providers).
verdicts.evidence: SST has said this in several of its own places. The SST Providers docs say "SST is built on Pulumi/Terraform and supports 150+ providers." The v3 launch post describes "a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform," and the v3 README says "It uses Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation."
verdicts.source: https://sst.dev/docs/providers/ ; https://sst.dev/blog/sst-v3/ ; https://github.com/degu-io/ion (mirror of SST v3 README)
verdicts.framing_note: SST's own wording is "built on Pulumi/Terraform" and "uses Pulumi and Terraform". The phrases "Pulumi engine" and "embedded engine plus Terraform-bridged providers" are the author's gloss, not SST's words. That gloss matches third-party descriptions and does not overstate what SST says. The multiple SST pages support "repeatedly."
verdicts.intuition_flag: The parenthetical technical detail comes from the author, not SST. Consider putting it outside the attribution.

verdicts.text: With SST you define an app's infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites, etc.), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
verdicts.evidence: The SST homepage shows an `sst.config.ts` example that uses SST components (`sst.aws.Email`, `sst.aws.Service`, `sst.aws.Nextjs`) and says "Deploy everything your app needs with a single config." The truncated body doesn't mention the `sst deploy` command or the specific examples "functions, queues, buckets."
verdicts.framing_note: The source says "Deploy everything your app needs with a single config" next to an sst.config.ts example, which matches the claim's core point. The `sst deploy` command and the listed component examples aren't in the fetched excerpt.

verdicts.text: In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's own v3 announcement (Aug 20, 2024) says: "Late last year we started work on a new deployment engine that would use Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation." It also says: "This new deployment engine, code named Ion". "Last year" relative to 2024 means late 2023.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "new deployment engine" replacing CDK/CloudFormation. The claim says "rewrite that replaced SST's entire deployment layer". That is the same assertion in slightly stronger words.

verdicts.text: SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" (https://sst.dev/blog/moving-away-from-cdk) states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."
verdicts.evidence: The fetched page contains the quote word for word: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi ; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."
verdicts.framing_note: The quote matches the source exactly, and the title "Moving away from CDK" is right. The only difference is a stray space before the semicolon in the fetched text, which is an HTML link artifact.

verdicts.text: SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
verdicts.evidence: The cited page loaded (HTTP 200), but the pre-fetched body cuts off before the "How Does Ion Work" section, so the exact quoted sentence could not be seen. The part that did load is consistent with the claim: "The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi".
verdicts.framing_note: The quote most likely sits in the "How Does Ion Work" section, which was not included in the fetched text. The visible content supports the general idea.

verdicts.text: The SST docs page "What is SST" (https://sst.dev/docs/) states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
verdicts.evidence: https://sst.dev/docs/ returned HTTP 200 and the title is "What is SST", but the fetched body was cut off in the navigation menu before any page text. The quoted sentence about Pulumi and Terraform providers does not appear in what was fetched, so I can't confirm it.
verdicts.framing_note: The page title "What is SST" matches the claim, but the pre-fetched body stops before the article text.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The quote sounds like real SST docs wording, but it may come from a different SST page (such as Providers or How it works) rather than the /docs/ intro.

verdicts.text: Independent developers who have compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture (SST built on the Pulumi engine).
verdicts.evidence: Independent third-party comparisons of SST, Terraform and Pulumi describe the same architecture. cdkbase says SST v3 "rebuilt on the Pulumi engine with Terraform providers underneath," and Encore calls SST "a higher-level layer on top of Pulumi."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is a general appeal to independent comparisons and names no specific source (source_hint "That"). Several independent comparison articles match its description. The Gautier Blandin Terraform/Pulumi/SST comparison snippets did not state this architecture.

verdicts.text: Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" states: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
verdicts.evidence: The page loaded (HTTP 200), but the pre-fetched body is cut off inside the Pulumi section, before the SST section, so I couldn't confirm the quoted sentence. Separately, the page's actual title is "Terraform vs Pulumi vs SST — A tradeoffs analysis" (published March 12, 2025), not "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" as the claim gives it.
verdicts.framing_note: Couldn't check the quote itself because the body was truncated. The article title is misquoted: the source has "Terraform vs Pulumi vs SST / A tradeoffs analysis"; the claim has "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis".
verdicts.intuition_flag: The article title in the blog post doesn't match the source page's title and should be corrected.

verdicts.text: Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" states: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
verdicts.evidence: The page returned HTTP 200 and confirms the author and title ("headline":"SST Ditches AWS CDK: Time to Move on to Ion", author "Kiryl Anoshka"). The fetched body is cut off before the quoted sentence about Pulumi imports, so I couldn't check the quote word for word.
verdicts.framing_note: Author and title are confirmed. The quote itself isn't in the fetched portion of the page. The claim writes the title as "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion"; the page has "SST Ditches AWS CDK: Time to Move on to Ion", a small difference in punctuation and capitalization.

verdicts.text: The published `platform/package.json` of SST's platform package (in the anomalyco/sst repository, formerly sst/sst) lists as direct dependencies `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel`.
verdicts.evidence: The fetched platform/package.json "dependencies" block lists all eight packages: "@pulumi/aws": "7.20.0", "@pulumi/cloudflare": "6.15.0", "@pulumi/command": "1.0.1", "@pulumi/docker-build": "0.0.14", "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0", "@pulumi/random": "4.16.6", "@pulumi/tls": "5.0.1", "@pulumiverse/vercel": "4.6.0". The "formerly sst/sst" rename detail isn't shown in the file body, so it wasn't checked.
verdicts.framing_note: All eight named packages appear under "dependencies", not devDependencies. The file also has other non-Pulumi dependencies, but the claim doesn't say the list is complete.

verdicts.text: The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside the Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).
verdicts.evidence: anomalyco/sst platform/package.json (@sst/platform) lists "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0", "@pulumi/aws": "7.20.0", "@pulumi/cloudflare": "6.15.0", "@pulumi/docker-build": "0.0.14", plus @pulumi/command, random, tls, and "@pulumiverse/vercel": "4.6.0".

verdicts.text: In SST, `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST's own components, and those components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say the sst.config.ts run function is "where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components". They also say a component's `nodes` property "contains references to the underlying Pulumi components that are created". The SST source architecture notes that components "generate underlying Pulumi resources".
verdicts.framing_note: SST docs describe SST components as wrappers that create underlying Pulumi components/resources. The claim's "compile into Pulumi resource declarations" is a loose paraphrase: at runtime they instantiate Pulumi ComponentResources rather than compiling in a literal sense.

verdicts.text: SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs say its built-in AWS components "Internally they use Pulumi's AWS provider," and that SST is "built on Pulumi/Terraform." This confirms that SST components end up as Pulumi resources.
verdicts.framing_note: Source says components 'internally use Pulumi's AWS provider'. The claim says 'compile into Pulumi resource declarations'. 'Compile' is figurative, since the components are Pulumi components that create resources at runtime, but the meaning holds.
verdicts.intuition_flag: 'Compile' suggests a code-generation step. SST components actually create Pulumi resources when the program runs, so 'map to' or 'are built from' would be more precise.

verdicts.text: In SST, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
verdicts.evidence: SST's own docs and third-party sources confirm that SST v3 uses Pulumi as its deployment engine. One source says SST "uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine". Diffing, building a dependency graph, and ordering operations are standard Pulumi engine behavior, and one source notes that Pulumi "performs parallel operations and skips no-op resources."
verdicts.framing_note: Sources say SST uses the Pulumi deployment engine. The claim adds the engine's standard diff, dependency-graph, and ordering steps, which follow from that.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Pulumi diffs the desired state against the last recorded state in its state file. It only compares against actual cloud state after a refresh, so "actual state" is slightly loose wording.

verdicts.text: Terraform-bridged providers (via Pulumi's Terraform bridge, github.com/pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) translate each resource into cloud API calls.
verdicts.evidence: The cited URL loads (HTTP 200) and is the right target. Its title reads "pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge: A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi.", which confirms the link names Pulumi's Terraform bridge. The fetched text was cut short and doesn't mention how bridged providers turn resources into cloud API calls.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says 'A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi', which backs the link's identity. The claim's point that each resource is translated into cloud API calls is standard provider behavior but isn't in the fetched text.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs underneath SST, while SST owns the CLI, component model, and local dev loop.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Independent sources say SST v3 uses Pulumi for the deployment engine and providers, including Terraform providers bridged through Pulumi. They also say SST ships its own CLI and its own components that wrap Pulumi: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine" (atomicobject), and "Only the SST CLI is installed" (mamezou). No source I found spells out the claim's exact split of duties (dependency resolution, preview/diff, state, local dev loop), but everything found is consistent with it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Hundreds of provider APIs" is a loose count. It's plausible because Terraform-bridged providers are available, but no source confirmed the number.

verdicts.text: AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
verdicts.evidence: By 2022, AWS said CloudFormation already covered "170+ AWS services spanning over 900 resource types". A current third-party catalog lists "all 1613 AWS CloudFormation resource types across 280 services", so "hundreds" is a safe lower bound. It understates the real count.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The actual count is over 1,000 (about 1,600 CloudFormation types). "Hundreds" is conservative, and the author could say "over a thousand" for precision.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's engine can run without a Pulumi account, without a network call to Pulumi Cloud, and without any Pulumi-hosted service.
verdicts.evidence: The state docs list DIY backends that need no Pulumi Cloud: "a 'Do It Yourself' backend that stores state in an object store you manage—AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, an S3-compatible server such as Minio or Ceph, a PostgreSQL database, or your local filesystem." Some caveats remain: by default the CLI checks for updates and downloads plugins from Pulumi-hosted endpoints such as get.pulumi.com. Both can be avoided (PULUMI_SKIP_UPDATE_CHECK, pre-installed plugins), but "without any Pulumi-hosted service" is only true once they are.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The absolute "without any Pulumi-hosted service" skips over the default plugin downloads and update checks that go to Pulumi endpoints.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside other teams' own tools, in the same embedded way SST embeds the engine.
verdicts.evidence: The Automation API docs say it lets you "drive the Pulumi engine from within your own application instead of invoking the `pulumi` command from a shell," and list "Building higher-level tools, such as custom CLIs over Pulumi" as a use case. That supports the claim that teams embed Pulumi inside their own tools. The docs also note that "Automation API drives the Pulumi CLI under the hood," so the CLI binary has to be available at runtime.
verdicts.framing_note: The docs describe driving the engine from your own application and building tools on top of Pulumi. The docs page doesn't mention SST, so the "same way SST does" comparison can't be checked against it.

verdicts.text: A docs page exists at /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ about consuming Terraform providers directly in Pulumi.
verdicts.evidence: The file content/docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers.md exists, so it serves /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/. Its title is "Use Terraform Providers", and it says "you can use any Terraform provider in your Pulumi programs" through `pulumi package add terraform-provider`.
verdicts.framing_note: The source_hint (/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/) is a different link, so this claim was checked only against its own target path.

verdicts.text: Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing their own.
verdicts.evidence: The repo page describes the project as "A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi." That supports the core fact that Terraform providers get reused in Pulumi. It says nothing about the bridge being built specifically for projects like SST.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source says 'A library allowing Terraform providers to be bridged into Pulumi', but the claim says it was 'built specifically to let projects like SST reuse' those providers. The bridge's main purpose is Pulumi's own bridged providers; downstream projects like SST benefit indirectly.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Saying the bridge was 'built specifically' for third-party projects like SST attributes an intent the source doesn't state.

verdicts.text: Cross-reference: the blog post /blog/any-terraform-provider/ exists and is titled "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi".
verdicts.evidence: The live page at https://www.pulumi.com/blog/any-terraform-provider/ exists, and its title is "Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi | Pulumi Blog". The part before the site suffix matches the claimed title word for word.
verdicts.framing_note: The page title minus the " | Pulumi Blog" suffix is the same as the title given in the claim.

verdicts.text: A docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ describing the Automation API for embedding Pulumi in other tools.
verdicts.evidence: content/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api.md exists, so it renders at /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/. It is titled "Automation API", and its meta_desc reads "The Pulumi Automation API is a programmatic interface for running Pulumi programs without the Pulumi CLI." That fits the blog's "embedding Pulumi in other tools" description.
verdicts.framing_note: The page says "programmatic interface for running Pulumi programs without the Pulumi CLI"; the claim's "embedding Pulumi in other tools" is a fair paraphrase of that.

verdicts.text: By embedding the Pulumi engine, SST gets a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers without building either from scratch.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Terraform bridge README says it "adapts any Terraform Provider… for use with Pulumi" and "connects the Pulumi engine to a given Terraform Provider using Pulumi's RPC interfaces." That backs up the idea that a tool embedding the engine gets the whole bridged provider catalog without building it. I couldn't check SST's own statements about embedding the engine from here: they only appear in the post's quotes from sst.dev.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The same post (L45) says SST deploys to "AWS and more than 150 other providers," so "hundreds of cloud providers" at L85 may overstate what SST actually ships.

verdicts.text: Nitric's own docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
verdicts.evidence: The cited nitric.io homepage returned HTTP 200 but does not include the quoted sentence. The page now promotes Suga ("Suga is what came out of it: hosting for agents, apps, and platforms") and links to docs.suga.app. It says nothing about deployment providers or Pulumi.
verdicts.framing_note: The cited page is the homepage, not a docs page. The quote probably comes from a Nitric docs page about providers, so the citation should link to that page directly.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Nitric's homepage has been rebranded to Suga, so the Nitric docs may have moved or been archived. Check that the quote still exists at a live URL.

verdicts.text: Defang's Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described by Defang as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
verdicts.evidence: The fetched page (HTTP 200) is truncated to the repo title only: "Defang Pulumi providers - Take your app from Docker Compose to a secure and scalable cloud deployment with Pulumi." The quoted wording "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" does not appear in what was fetched, so I couldn't confirm it.
verdicts.framing_note: The repo description supports the general idea (Docker Compose → cloud deployment with Pulumi), but it does not contain the verbatim quote that the claim attributes to Defang.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The text is presented as a direct Defang quote, but the repo tagline says it differently. It may be the author's paraphrase shown in quotation marks. Check the README for the exact wording.

verdicts.text: Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Nitric's docs say that "All of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments", using the Pulumi Automation API. Defang's CLI runs BYOC deployments through Pulumi: its source has a `PulumiStack`, a Pulumi backend setting, and a pulumi-defang CD program. Neither source mentions the "provider bridge" by name. It follows only by inference, because the Pulumi AWS/GCP/Azure providers they rely on are bridged.
verdicts.framing_note: Nitric also has Terraform-based IaC providers, so it doesn't rely on Pulumi only. Pulumi is the engine behind its default direct-deployment providers.

verdicts.text: Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code; they work entirely in SST's component model.
verdicts.evidence: No public source puts a number on how many SST users write Pulumi code directly. SST's docs back the general idea that the Pulumi engine is embedded ("You don't need to install Pulumi or sign up for it, their engine is embedded in the Ion CLI") and that SST components "Internally … use Pulumi's AWS provider", but that doesn't establish "most users".
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "SST v3 built on Pulumi users don't need to know Pulumi"; https://sst.dev/blog/moving-away-from-cdk/; https://sst.dev/docs/components/
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Most users never write a line of Pulumi code" is a claim about how many users do something, with no survey or data behind it. SST also offers direct Pulumi/Terraform providers and transforms, so some users do write Pulumi resources. Consider softening to "Many SST users…" or "SST users don't need to write Pulumi code".

verdicts.text: Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, users can define raw Pulumi resources directly inside an SST app, for resources without a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app.
verdicts.evidence: SST's config reference says the run function is "where you define your resources using SST or Pulumi's components". Its providers docs add that "Aside from the built-in components, SST supports any of the 150+ Pulumi and Terraform providers." So you can put raw Pulumi resources alongside SST components in the same app and deploy them together.
verdicts.framing_note: The SST docs say both SST and Pulumi components can be defined in run(). The claim's use case (resources that have no SST component) is a special case of that. SST v3 calls these "components", not "constructs", which is CDK/v2 wording.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Constructs" is SST v2/CDK wording. SST v3 calls them "components", so the author may want to change the word.

verdicts.text: Anyone who runs SST is already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not they have written any Pulumi code.
verdicts.evidence: SST's current platform package (sst/sst platform/package.json) depends directly on "@pulumi/pulumi": "3.215.0" and on first-party Pulumi providers (@pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, etc.). So every SST v3 deploy goes through the Pulumi engine, even for users who only write SST components. The universal "anyone" is only true for v3: legacy SST v2 ran on CDK/CloudFormation. The post itself says v3 "has been the only supported architecture since" mid-2024.

verdicts.text: SST is a strong fit if you want an opinionated, full-stack application framework with infrastructure and code defined together; Pulumi directly makes more sense once you need cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application, capabilities SST doesn't expose on its own.

This backs the cross-team visibility and policy points, but the page says nothing about SST, so the claim that SST doesn't offer these features isn't checked here.

verdicts.text: Yes. Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) SST's SST v3 announcement (dated Aug 20, 2024) says "Ion is now officially being released as SST v3" and that "SST was built on AWS CDK and CloudFormation". It describes the new engine as using "Pulumi and Terraform, as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation."
verdicts.framing_note: The August 20, 2024 release fits "mid-2024" loosely (it's closer to late summer). SST's Jan 2024 post confirms components are "defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi".

verdicts.text: SST's components are defined using Terraform providers that are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
verdicts.evidence: SST's docs say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi." SST's v3 post also says state "is stored locally and backed up to S3", and a third-party write-up notes that only the SST CLI needs to be installed. No source says outright that SST never calls the Terraform CLI or writes Terraform state. That part is inferred from the Pulumi-engine design.
verdicts.framing_note: The source says 'Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi' and SST uses Pulumi's deployment engine. The claim's 'no Terraform CLI / no Terraform state' part is a reasonable reading of that, but no source states it directly. Also, SST components wrap Pulumi providers, and many of those providers are bridged from Terraform, so 'defined using Terraform providers' simplifies things a little.
